preview.heading: Study in the Home of World-Class Education
preview.paragraph:
With over 160 universities to choose from, the UK gives you a range of study options few other countries can match. From world-renowned historic institutions to modern, industry-focused campuses, you can shape a degree around your own goals rather than someone else's template.

Beyond the classroom, you'll find an open, multicultural way of life, dependable transport connecting every corner of the country, and one of the most respected healthcare systems in the world.

details.introParagraph: Beyond the world-class education and high-quality teaching, there is so much to love in the UK (also known by its full name: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland). From our open and inclusive way of life to our ancient traditions, and our stunning landscapes to our unbeatable international cultural scene, you'll be well looked after — with a trustworthy police force, affordable transport connecting towns and cities across all four nations, and one of the most advanced healthcare systems in the world.

highlight.title: UK Nations
highlight.body:
The UK is a union of four nations — England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales — each with its own character, cities, and traditions. Studying in Manchester feels very different to studying in Edinburgh or Cardiff, and that variety means you can pick a setting that genuinely fits how you want to live, not just where the highest-ranked course happens to be.

Every nation shares the same world-class standard of teaching and the same post-study opportunities, so the choice comes down to the kind of city, pace, and culture you want around you for the next few years.

topics.title: Food
topics.body:
UK food culture is far more diverse than its reputation suggests. Every major city has thriving international food scenes — from South Asian and Middle Eastern to East African and Caribbean — sitting alongside British classics like a Sunday roast or fish and chips.

Student budgets go a long way if you cook at home: supermarkets like Aldi, Lidl, and Tesco offer weekly essentials at low prices, and most campuses have affordable halls kitchens or student-priced cafés. Eating out is easiest to manage with lunchtime deals, student discount apps, and local markets, which are usually cheaper and fresher than city-centre chains.

topics.title: Weather
topics.body:
UK weather is genuinely changeable — a bright morning can turn into an afternoon drizzle without much warning, which is exactly why locals treat a light rain jacket as a year-round essential rather than a seasonal one.

Summers are mild (usually 18–25°C) and winters rarely drop far below freezing outside of the north, but the damp and the shorter daylight hours in winter take some adjusting to for students coming from hotter climates. A good waterproof coat, layers you can add or remove through the day, and sturdy shoes will get you through almost any UK forecast comfortably.

topics.title: Religion
topics.body:
The UK is a multi-faith, largely secular society where all religions are widely practised and respected. Most university towns and cities have mosques, temples, gurdwaras, churches, and synagogues within easy reach of campus, and student unions typically run dedicated faith and cultural societies.

Universities are generally well set up to support religious students — think prayer rooms on campus, halal and other dietary options in dining halls, and flexibility around religious holidays for coursework and exams. It's worth checking your specific university's faith and chaplaincy services once you have an offer.

topics.title: Travel and Transport
topics.body:
Whether you're based in a city centre or a quieter campus town, the UK's transport network makes it easy to get around — and to see a lot of the country during your time here. Buses and trains connect virtually every town, and most cities have local discount travel cards for students.

A 16-25 Railcard cuts train fares by up to a third, and many local bus operators offer similar student passes. For weekend trips, budget coach services and regional trains make cities like Edinburgh, Manchester, Bristol, and Cardiff easily reachable without needing a car — most students never own one during their studies.

topics.title: Language
topics.body:
English is spoken and taught across the UK, but it isn't the only language you'll hear on a daily basis. In London alone, it's estimated that more than 300 languages are spoken, and most university cities have similarly diverse international communities.

Welsh, Scottish Gaelic, and Irish are also official languages in their respective nations, visible on road signs and public announcements in parts of Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. For international students, most universities also offer English-language support courses alongside your degree if you want extra confidence in academic writing or spoken English.

topics.title: Holidays
topics.body:
The UK calendar is full of public holidays and local celebrations worth planning around — from Christmas markets and New Year fireworks to Bonfire Night, Pancake Day, and regional festivals unique to each nation, like St Andrew's Day in Scotland or St David's Day in Wales.

Universities typically build these into the academic calendar with a winter break around Christmas and New Year and a spring break around Easter, giving international students a natural window to travel home or explore Europe. Term-time also brings university-run cultural events, so you don't have to wait for an official holiday to experience UK traditions firsthand.

whyStudy.summary: Beyond the rankings, here's what actually matters day-to-day: what it costs to live, how easy it is to work part-time, and what happens after you graduate.

reasons.heading: World-Class Universities, Recognised Everywhere
reasons.body:
The UK is home to some of the most respected universities on the planet, including Oxford, Cambridge, and Imperial College London — names that carry weight with employers no matter where in the world you end up working. What makes UK teaching stand out isn't just the ranking, though; it's the style of teaching itself, which pushes students to think critically, question ideas, and form their own opinions rather than just memorise facts.

With one of the widest ranges of subjects available anywhere, whatever you choose to study, you'll be learning it at a genuinely high standard.

reasons.heading: Shorter Degrees, Lower Overall Cost
reasons.body:
One thing that surprises a lot of international students: a UK Master's degree usually takes just one year, and a Bachelor's takes three — both shorter than the norm in countries like the US or Canada. That shorter timeline doesn't mean a lighter education; it just means a more focused one.

It also has a very practical upside — less time spent studying means less money spent on tuition and living costs overall, so your degree ends up more affordable even before you factor in scholarships or part-time work.

reasons.heading: Stay and Work After You Graduate
reasons.body:
Finishing your degree doesn't mean your time in the UK has to end. The Graduate Route visa lets international students stay on for up to 18 months after an undergraduate or Master's degree — or 3 years after a PhD — to work or look for work, with no job offer required to apply.

This gives you real breathing room to build UK work experience, grow your professional network, and — if things go well — move into a longer-term skilled worker visa with an employer willing to sponsor you.

reasons.heading: Earn While You Learn
reasons.body:
Studying in the UK doesn't mean putting your finances entirely on hold. Most international students on a Student visa can work up to 20 hours a week during term time, and full-time during holidays — enough to cover some day-to-day costs and pick up valuable UK work experience along the way.

Common options include retail, hospitality, and on-campus roles like library or student ambassador positions. It's not usually enough to fund your studies on its own, but it takes some pressure off your budget.

reasons.heading: A Safe, Welcoming, Multicultural Home
reasons.body:
With students arriving from over 180 countries, UK campuses are genuinely international places — you'll find classmates, food, festivals, and faith communities from all over the world, often within walking distance of each other. Whatever your background or beliefs, there's a strong chance you'll feel at home quickly.

Universities also back this up with real support — pastoral teams who help with everything from housing and visa questions to homesickness and language confidence — plus a low crime rate and a trustworthy police force that make everyday life feel secure.

reasons.heading: Healthcare You Don't Have to Worry About
reasons.body:
Health cover is one less thing to stress about while you're studying abroad. As part of your student visa application, you'll pay the Immigration Health Surcharge, which then gives you access to the UK's National Health Service (NHS) — one of the most comprehensive public healthcare systems in the world.

That covers both physical and mental health care, so if you ever need to see a doctor, get treatment, or talk to someone about how you're coping, help is there and it's affordable.

reasons.heading: A Head Start on a Global Career
reasons.body:
UK graduates are known for being genuinely job-ready — it isn't unusual for students to receive offers before they've even finished their final year. Employers don't just value the qualification on paper; they consistently point to strong English communication, sharp problem-solving, and confident leadership as what sets UK graduates apart.

A lot of that comes from how closely UK universities work with industry — placements, internships, and guest input from real companies mean you're building professional connections and practical experience long before graduation, not just after it.

sections.title: Cost of Living
sections.summary: Monthly living costs in the UK typically range from £900–1,400, depending heavily on the city — London runs noticeably higher than most other regions.
sections.body: Accommodation is usually the biggest expense, whether in university halls or private rentals. Outside London, students often manage on £900–1,100/month covering rent, food, transport, and essentials. In London, that figure regularly climbs toward £1,300–1,400/month. Budgeting for the first month is especially important, since many rentals ask for a deposit plus a month's rent upfront.

sections.title: Part-time Job Opportunities
sections.summary: Most international students on a Student visa can work up to 20 hours per week during term time, and full-time during holidays.
sections.body: Common part-time roles for students include retail, hospitality, campus jobs (library assistant, student ambassador), and tutoring. Pay is usually around the National Minimum Wage. It's worth noting that part-time income is rarely enough to fully cover living costs on its own — it's best treated as a supplement, not a primary funding source. Visa conditions around working hours should always be checked directly against your specific visa type before accepting any job.

sections.title: After Graduation
sections.summary: Graduates can apply for the Graduate Route visa, allowing up to 18 months (3 years for PhD graduates) to work or job-hunt in the UK after finishing a degree.
sections.body: The Graduate Route doesn't require a job offer to apply — it simply extends your stay so you can look for work, gain experience, or transition into a skilled worker visa later if you find a sponsoring employer. Career services at most UK universities offer CV reviews, interview practice, and employer networking events, which are worth using well before your final semester.

topCourses.name: Economics
topCourses.body: Economics tops the list for international applicants, drawing the highest volume of overseas applications of any subject. It blends maths-heavy analysis with real-world topics — inflation, productivity, market behaviour, budgeting — and pairs well with joint degrees like Economics & Finance or Politics, Philosophy & Economics. That flexibility is a big part of the appeal: the skill set transfers cleanly into government, global business, education, or finance, which is likely why it consistently pulls in such a wide international applicant pool.

topCourses.name: Law
topCourses.body: Law is the second most applied-to subject among international students, largely thanks to the UK's outsized influence on legal systems worldwide — English common law underpins a huge share of legal frameworks globally, and English commercial law shapes how many international contracts are written. A Law degree sharpens research, analytical thinking, negotiation, and communication skills, and strong English proficiency matters a lot here. It opens doors well beyond courtrooms — business, government, and community-facing careers all draw on a legal background.

topCourses.name: Computer Science
topCourses.body: Computer Science ranks third by application volume, and it's easy to see why given the strong graduate earning potential attached to it. Students go on to work across software, computing architecture, VR, e-commerce platforms, and robotics, backed by well-regarded UK computer science departments and researchers. Since nearly every industry now runs on some form of computer system, graduate outcomes in this field tend to stay strong across a wide range of career paths.

topCourses.name: Management Studies
topCourses.body: Management Studies is the single most popular business-related subject for international students, focused on how organisations actually run — strategy, structure, decision-making, and the practical mechanics of finance, marketing, and HR. Because the skills are largely industry-agnostic, graduates have a lot of flexibility when choosing where to build a career, which is a major part of why this subject draws such a large applicant pool every year.

topCourses.name: Design Studies
topCourses.body: Design Studies suits students who enjoy solving problems in a visual, hands-on way — the subject spans everything from graphic and industrial design to fashion and textiles. Alongside discipline-specific technique, students build practical skills in computer-aided design and get real experience responding to client-style briefs, which keeps the degree closely tied to how design work actually happens in industry.

topCourses.name: Psychology
topCourses.body: Psychology is popular with UK and international students alike — it's the study of how people think, feel, and behave, covering both the science behind the mind and the research methods used to study it. Beyond subject knowledge, it builds strong critical thinking, problem-solving, and data-handling skills, and it opens into a genuinely wide range of careers, from clinical psychology and therapy to research and data analysis roles.

topCourses.name: Politics
topCourses.body: Politics stays relevant no matter where a student is from, which likely explains its consistent popularity with international applicants. Studying it in the UK means direct exposure to a dense political landscape — active parties, legislative institutions, think tanks, and NGOs — alongside strong research expertise at UK universities. Most programmes also allow real flexibility to tailor the degree toward a student's specific interests within the field.

topCourses.name: Business and Management
topCourses.body: For students who can't quite decide between a pure Business or Management degree, this combined subject covers both — how a business operates as an organisation and the wider environment it operates within. It's also commonly studied alongside another subject entirely, with popular combinations including Economics, Information Systems, and International Studies, giving students room to specialise while keeping a broad business foundation.

topCourses.name: Medicine
topCourses.body: Medicine draws a huge number of applications, but it's also by far the most competitive subject on this list — only a small share of international applicants receive an offer. UK Medicine degrees are held to strict standards set by the General Medical Council, many give students early exposure to real patients, and the research environment at UK medical schools is genuinely world-class. Given how competitive entry is, it's worth going in with a backup plan — whether that's a graduate-entry route later or a related career path.

topCourses.name: Business Studies
topCourses.body: Business Studies rounds out the top ten and is the broadest of the three business-related entries on this list, covering economics, accounting, marketing, and management in one degree. It builds skills that carry across almost any industry — from how a workplace is organised to how people and resources are managed — making it a practical, flexible starting point for students who know they want a business career but aren't yet sure which corner of it.

entryRequirements.undergraduate: Typically A-Levels (grades roughly BBB to AAA depending on how competitive the course is) or an equivalent qualification like the IB (around 32–38 points), plus English proficiency — usually IELTS 6.0–6.5 overall.
entryRequirements.postgraduate: Usually a 2:1 Bachelor's degree (or equivalent GPA) in a related subject, plus English proficiency — typically IELTS 6.5–7.0 overall, sometimes higher for competitive courses like Law or Medicine.

intakes.name: September — Main Intake
intakes.detail: The main intake, with by far the widest choice of courses, accommodation, and student life. The main UCAS deadline for most undergraduate courses is mid-January (around 15 January) for that year's September start — but Oxford, Cambridge, and Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary courses close earlier, around mid-October.

intakes.name: January — Second Intake
intakes.detail: A smaller intake — not every university or course offers a January start. Useful if you missed the September deadline, need more time to arrange your visa finances, or specifically want to start mid-year, though course choice is more limited.

faqs.question: What English score do I need, and can I apply without IELTS?
faqs.answer:
Most UK universities ask for around IELTS 6.0–6.5 overall for undergraduate courses and 6.5–7.0 for postgraduate ones, with higher scores for subjects like Law or Medicine. IELTS isn't the only route, though — many universities also accept TOEFL, PTE, the Duolingo English Test, their own English test, or a Medium of Instruction (MOI) letter if your previous degree was taught in English.

One thing to watch: getting a waiver from the university doesn't automatically settle your visa. Your university has to confirm your English level when it issues your CAS, so ask them exactly what they'll accept before you pay for any test.

faqs.question: How much money do I need to show for the student visa?
faqs.answer:
You need to show two amounts: your first-year tuition fee that's still unpaid, plus living costs for up to nine months. Right now the living-cost figure is £1,529 a month for London and £1,171 a month outside London — roughly £13,761 and £10,539 over nine months. These go up for applications made on or after 30 November 2026, to £1,570 and £1,203 a month.

The money needs to stay in your account for at least 28 days in a row before you apply. The visa fee (£558) and the Immigration Health Surcharge (£776 per year of your visa) are separate, so keep a little extra on top.

faqs.question: Are there scholarships for international students?
faqs.answer:
Yes, but competition is strong, so it pays to look early. The best-known are Chevening (UK government, fully funded one-year master's, with applications usually opening around August), Commonwealth Scholarships (for students from eligible Commonwealth countries) and GREAT Scholarships (at least £10,000 towards tuition for a one-year master's, for students from selected countries, applied for through participating universities).

On top of these, most universities run their own merit awards and bursaries, often with smaller applicant pools. Some are considered automatically when you apply; others have a deadline soon after your offer. Government scholarships can close 9–12 months before the course starts, so check dates well ahead of your application.

faqs.question: When should I start applying?
faqs.answer:
Start about 9–12 months before your course begins. For a September start, the main UCAS deadline for most undergraduate courses is around 15 January, while Oxford, Cambridge and Medicine, Dentistry and Veterinary courses close earlier, around mid-October. Postgraduate applications go straight to the university, and popular courses can fill up before any official deadline.

Applying early also gives you a better shot at scholarships and university accommodation. Once you hold an offer and your CAS, you can apply for the visa — it's usually decided in about three weeks from outside the UK, but leave extra time in case documents are queried.

faqs.question: Can I bring my spouse or children with me?
faqs.answer:
For most students, no. Since 1 January 2024, only students on PhD or other research-based postgraduate courses lasting nine months or more — and government-sponsored students — can bring a partner or children. If you're on a bachelor's or taught master's course, dependants can't join you on a Student visa.

If you do qualify, each family member needs their own visa application and extra funds shown on top of yours. It's worth checking this before you choose a course, because it can change which programme makes sense for your family.

faqs.question: Where will I live, and how much will it cost?
faqs.answer:
Many first-year international students start in university halls, which are the simplest option — bills are often included and you're close to campus. Other choices are private student accommodation (purpose-built blocks) or a room in a shared house.

Prices vary a lot by city. University halls average around £190 a week across the UK and closer to £280 in London, while a room in a shared house is often cheaper, though bills may be extra. Book as early as you can once you have an offer — the better-value rooms tend to go first.

faqs.question: What if my visa application is refused?
faqs.answer:
A refusal isn't always the end of the road. Your refusal letter will explain exactly why, so read it carefully and tell your university right away — they can advise you and, if a fresh application makes sense, issue a new CAS (the old one can't be reused after a refusal).

There's no general right of appeal for a Student visa applied for from outside the UK. If you believe the Home Office made a mistake, you can ask for an administrative review within 28 days. That can take a long time, though, so many students find it faster to fix the problem — for example, the funds or a missing document — and apply again.

faqs.question: Can I apply on my own, or do I need a consultancy?
faqs.answer:
You can absolutely apply on your own — universities accept direct applications, undergraduate courses go through UCAS, and the visa is applied for on the official GOV.UK website. Plenty of students do it themselves.

The catch is that there are many moving parts: choosing the right course, meeting deadlines, timing your funds for the 28-day rule, getting your CAS, and preparing visa documents. Small mistakes here are a common reason applications get delayed or refused. A good counsellor can save you time and catch problems early — and if you'd like a second pair of eyes on your plan, that's exactly what our team is here for.

courses.guidanceIntro: The UK offers thousands of undergraduate and postgraduate courses. When deciding on a course, it helps to think about your academic and career goals, whether the course offers work placements or research opportunities, and what current or former students say about their experience.
guidanceQuestions: What subject are you most interested in, and how does it align with your future ambitions?
Does the course include work placements or a semester abroad (undergraduate) or research opportunities and industry connections (postgraduate)?
Would you prefer to study full-time or part-time?
What are the entry requirements for your level of study?
What do current and former students say about their experience in this course?

preview.heading: Study in a Country Known for Its Welcome
preview.paragraph:
Canada has high-quality universities and colleges spread across ten provinces and three territories, from big, busy cities to quieter campus towns. You can pick a setting that fits how you want to live, and study in English, in French, or in both.

Outside the classroom you'll find a safe, multicultural society, well-run public services, and plenty of open space for weekends away.

details.introParagraph: Beyond the strong teaching and well-regarded degrees, there is a lot to like about life in Canada. It is a country built by people from all over the world, and that shows in its neighbourhoods, food, festivals and everyday attitudes. Cities are safe and easy to settle into, public transport is widespread, and nature is never far away, whether that means a lake, a mountain trail or a quiet beach. Winters are cold, but campuses and cities are well set up for them, and most international students find the welcome warmer than the weather.

highlight.title: Provinces and Territories
highlight.body:
Canada is made up of ten provinces and three territories, each with its own character, climate and, in some cases, language. Most international students study in Ontario and British Columbia, home to cities like Toronto, Ottawa and Vancouver, but Quebec, Alberta, Nova Scotia and the Prairie provinces all have strong institutions and often lower living costs.

Education is run by each province, so tuition, health cover and the rules for attestation letters can differ depending on where you study. It's worth comparing provinces, not just universities, before you apply.

topics.title: Food
topics.body:
Canadian food is a mix of local favourites and flavours from around the world. You'll find poutine, maple syrup treats, butter tarts and Nanaimo bars, but also excellent South Asian, East Asian, Middle Eastern, Caribbean and African food in almost every big city. Halal, kosher and vegetarian options are easy to find in most university cities.

Student budgets stretch furthest if you cook at home. Supermarkets such as Walmart, No Frills and Costco keep everyday groceries affordable, and many campuses have student-priced cafés and food banks. A typical grocery budget is around C$200 to C$600 a month, depending on how often you eat out.

topics.title: Weather
topics.body:
Canada has four clear seasons. Summers are warm and sunny, autumn brings brilliant colours, and winters can be properly cold and snowy, especially in Ontario, Quebec and the Prairies, where temperatures often fall well below freezing. The Pacific coast, including Vancouver, is milder but wetter.

If you come from a warmer country, the first winter takes some adjusting to. A good winter coat, insulated waterproof boots, gloves and layers you can add or remove are worth buying early. Many cities, such as Toronto and Montreal, also have indoor walkways and underground networks that make winter days easier.

topics.title: Religion
topics.body:
Canada is a multi-faith, largely secular society where freedom of religion is protected and people of many beliefs live side by side. Most university cities have mosques, temples, gurdwaras, churches, synagogues and other places of worship within reach of campus, and student unions often run faith and cultural societies.

Campuses are generally well set up for religious students, with prayer and multi-faith spaces, chaplaincy services and dietary options in dining halls. It's worth checking the services at your specific university once you have an offer.

topics.title: Travel and Transport
topics.body:
Canada is huge, but getting around your own city is straightforward. Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and most other cities have buses, trains or subways, and many universities include a transit pass in student fees or offer a discounted one. A monthly transit pass is usually in the range of C$80 to C$150.

For trips between cities, distances are long, so most students use trains, intercity coaches or low-cost flights, and plan bigger trips for holidays. Most students don't need a car, and winter driving takes real experience, so it's best to wait until you know the area.

topics.title: Language
topics.body:
English and French are both official languages. Across most of Canada daily life and teaching happen in English, while Quebec is mainly French-speaking, and cities like Montreal, Ottawa and parts of New Brunswick are bilingual.

Most international students study in English, and several universities in Quebec teach in French. Learning some French can help with jobs and day-to-day life in those areas, and either language can be used to prove your level for study and work permits.

topics.title: Holidays
topics.body:
The Canadian calendar is full of celebrations worth planning around: Canada Day on 1 July, Thanksgiving in October, Remembrance Day on 11 November, Christmas and New Year, plus provincial holidays such as Family Day in February and Victoria Day in May. There are also local festivals, winter carnivals and music events almost every month.

Universities build a break around the winter holidays and a short reading week in the middle of term, which gives international students a natural window to travel or rest. The long summer break is a good chance to work, take a co-op placement or explore the country.

whyStudy.summary: Beyond the rankings, here's what matters day to day: what it costs to live, how much you can work while you study, and what you can do after you graduate.

reasons.heading: High-Quality Universities and Colleges, Respected Worldwide
reasons.body:
Canada is home to well-known research universities such as the University of Toronto, McGill and the University of British Columbia, alongside colleges that focus on practical, career-ready training. Employers around the world recognise Canadian qualifications, and teaching tends to be discussion-based, with plenty of group work and independent thinking.

Whether you want a research-heavy degree or a hands-on diploma, there is a route that fits, and many programmes let you build in work experience along the way.

reasons.heading: Good Value, Especially at Graduate Level
reasons.body:
Tuition depends a lot on the province and the programme. Statistics Canada's 2025/26 figures put the average for international undergraduates at about C$41,746 a year and for international graduate students at about C$24,028. Averages range widely: roughly C$18,867 for undergraduates in Newfoundland and Labrador, compared with about C$49,802 in Ontario.

That means choosing your province and programme carefully can change your total cost a great deal, and smaller cities often have lower rent too.

reasons.heading: Work While You Study
reasons.body:
If your study permit allows it, you can work off campus for up to 24 hours a week during term and full-time during scheduled breaks, and on-campus work is also possible. That can cover some day-to-day costs and give you real Canadian work experience before you graduate.

It isn't enough to fund your studies on its own, so treat it as a supplement. Always check your study permit conditions before you start a job.

reasons.heading: A Clear Route to Work After Graduation
reasons.body:
Many graduates can apply for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), which can last up to three years depending on the length of your programme. Graduates of a master's degree can receive the full three years even if the programme was shorter than two years, as long as they meet the other requirements.

Bachelor's, master's and doctoral graduates do not have to meet the field-of-study list, but you do need to prove your English or French level, and you can only receive one PGWP in your lifetime. Canadian work experience can also help later if you want to apply to stay long-term.

reasons.heading: A Safe, Welcoming, Multicultural Home
reasons.body:
Canada is one of the most diverse countries in the world, and international students quickly find classmates, food, festivals and communities from their own part of the world. Most campuses run orientation programmes, peer mentors and student services built around newcomers.

Cities are generally safe, public services work well, and people tend to be friendly and polite, which makes the first few weeks far easier.

reasons.heading: Study in English, French, or Both
reasons.body:
Canada has two official languages, which gives you choices most countries can't. Most students study in English, but you can also study in French in Quebec and bilingual regions, and many students pick up some French along the way.

Being able to work in two international languages is a real advantage on your CV, whether you stay in Canada or return home.

reasons.heading: Hands-On Learning and Industry Links
reasons.body:
Many Canadian programmes include co-op terms, internships or required work placements, so you graduate with experience as well as a degree. This is especially common in engineering, business, computer science and health programmes.

Recent rule changes mean most post-secondary international students no longer need a separate co-op work permit for placements that are a required part of their programme, but always confirm the details with your university's international office.

sections.title: Cost of Living
sections.summary: From 1 September 2026, a single study permit applicant must show C$23,448 for living costs, which works out to roughly C$1,950 a month, and many students spend more in Vancouver and Toronto.
sections.body: Rent is usually the biggest expense, and it varies a lot by city: it is highest in Vancouver and Toronto and generally lower in smaller cities. Food is often C$200 to C$600 a month, and a monthly transit pass is usually C$80 to C$150. Quebec sets its own, higher proof-of-funds amount for study permits, so students heading there should check the Quebec rules. Budget for your first month carefully, since landlords often ask for a deposit or advance rent.

sections.title: Part-time Job Opportunities
sections.summary: Eligible students can work up to 24 hours a week off campus during term, and full-time during scheduled breaks.
sections.body: Common student jobs include retail, hospitality, campus roles and tutoring. The 24-hour limit is strict, and working more than your permit allows can put your status at risk, so keep a record of your hours. Work is only allowed if your study permit says so, and you can't start working before your programme begins. Part-time income rarely covers all living costs, so it works best as a supplement.

sections.title: After Graduation
sections.summary: Graduates can apply for a Post-Graduation Work Permit of up to three years, depending on programme length.
sections.body: To qualify for a PGWP you need to graduate from an eligible programme at a designated learning institution, study full time, and meet the language requirement (CLB 7 for university degrees, CLB 5 for college programmes). You must apply within 180 days of getting confirmation that you've completed your programme. Career services at most Canadian universities offer CV help, interview practice and employer events, which are worth using well before your final term.

topCourses.name: Engineering
topCourses.body: Engineering is one of the most popular choices for international students in Canada, with civil, mechanical, electrical, software and chemical engineering all drawing strong interest. Canadian engineering degrees are widely recognised, many include co-op terms, and the skills carry across construction, energy, technology and manufacturing. It's a demanding subject, so check the maths and science requirements for your level before you apply.

topCourses.name: Business and Management
topCourses.body: Business and management remains one of the most popular fields of study among international students in Canada, from undergraduate business degrees to MBAs and specialist master's programmes in areas like marketing, supply chain and analytics. The skills are useful in almost any industry, and many programmes offer co-op or internship options that help you build a Canadian network.

topCourses.name: Computer Science
topCourses.body: Computer Science attracts a large share of international applicants, supported by strong research departments and a busy tech sector in cities like Toronto, Vancouver, Waterloo and Montreal. Programmes cover software, systems, security and more, and co-op streams are common. Because nearly every industry now depends on software, graduate options stay broad.

topCourses.name: Nursing
topCourses.body: Nursing is a popular route for students who want a career in health care, and Canada has an ongoing need for nurses. Entry is competitive, programmes include supervised clinical placements, and licensing as a nurse in Canada has extra steps beyond graduation, so it's worth checking the rules of the province where you want to work.

topCourses.name: Accounting and Finance
topCourses.body: Accounting and finance programmes appeal to students who want a clear professional path. Canadian business schools often link their degrees to professional accounting bodies and offer co-op placements with banks and firms. The skills are in demand across industries, and finance and accounting graduates have a wide choice of employers.

topCourses.name: Data Science
topCourses.body: Data science sits between statistics and computing, and interest in it among international students has grown quickly. Programmes teach how to collect, analyse and interpret data, often with machine learning and visualisation, and you'll find options at both undergraduate and master's level. It suits students who enjoy maths and problem-solving.

topCourses.name: Psychology
topCourses.body: Psychology is popular for its mix of science and social study, covering how people think, feel and behave. It builds research, statistics and communication skills that carry into health, education, human resources and data roles. Some careers, such as clinical practice, need further study and licensing, so it helps to know where you want to end up.

topCourses.name: Health Sciences
topCourses.body: Health sciences covers areas such as public health, biomedical science and rehabilitation, and it draws students who want a health career without going straight into medicine. Health-related fields have become a bigger share of international student interest in recent years. Many graduates go on to further study, research or roles in health systems and public health.

topCourses.name: Medicine
topCourses.body: Medicine attracts many applications, but places for international students are very limited and entry is among the most competitive of any subject, so only a small share of applicants receive an offer. Programmes follow strict professional standards, and practising in Canada after graduation involves licensing steps. It's wise to go in with a backup plan, such as a related health degree.

topCourses.name: Artificial Intelligence
topCourses.body: Artificial intelligence is one of the fastest-growing areas of study, and Canada has a strong research reputation in machine learning, with major research groups in cities like Toronto, Montreal and Edmonton. Programmes are mostly at master's and PhD level, though more undergraduate options are appearing, and a solid background in maths and programming helps.

entryRequirements.undergraduate: Typically a high school diploma or equivalent (such as A-Levels, the IB or a national board certificate) with strong grades in relevant subjects, plus English proficiency, often IELTS around 6.5 overall with no band below 6.0 for universities. Colleges often accept around IELTS 6.0. Requirements vary by programme, so check each one.
entryRequirements.postgraduate: Usually a four-year bachelor's degree in a related subject with a strong grade average, plus a statement of purpose and references, and English proficiency around IELTS 6.5 to 7.0. Research degrees may also need a supervisor to agree to take you on, and professional programmes can have extra requirements.

intakes.name: September: Main Intake
intakes.detail: The main intake, with the widest choice of programmes, scholarships and housing. Application deadlines for most universities fall somewhere between December and March for a September start, with some competitive programmes and scholarships closing earlier, so aim to apply 9 to 12 months ahead.

intakes.name: January: Second Intake
intakes.detail: Offered by many colleges and some universities, but with a smaller range of programmes. It's a useful option if you missed the September deadline or need more time to organise your funds and documents.

intakes.name: May: Smaller Intake
intakes.detail: A limited intake, mostly at colleges and for selected programmes. Not every institution offers it, so check early whether your chosen course starts in May.

faqs.question: What English score do I need, and which tests are accepted?
faqs.answer:
Most Canadian universities ask for around IELTS 6.5 overall for undergraduate courses and 6.5 to 7.0 for postgraduate ones, while many colleges accept around 6.0. Some universities also take TOEFL, PTE, the Duolingo English Test or a Medium of Instruction letter, so check each one.

There is a second language rule to know about: to receive a Post-Graduation Work Permit after a university degree, you need CLB 7, which is about IELTS 6.0 in each skill. For this you need to take an approved test such as IELTS General Training, CELPIP General or PTE Core, so it's worth planning for it before you finish your degree.

faqs.question: How much money do I need to show for the study permit?
faqs.answer:
You need to show you can pay your first year's tuition, living costs and travel to Canada. From 1 September 2026, the living-cost amount for a single applicant is C$23,448 (outside Quebec), and it is higher if you bring family. Quebec has its own, higher requirement, so check it if you plan to study there.

This figure doesn't include tuition. A Guaranteed Investment Certificate is a common way to show funds, but IRCC accepts other proof as well, such as bank statements. The study permit fee is C$150, with an extra C$85 for biometrics, so keep some money on top.

faqs.question: What is a Provincial Attestation Letter (PAL), and do I need one?
faqs.answer:
Canada limits the number of study permits it issues each year, and most new applicants must include a Provincial or Territorial Attestation Letter that shows they have a place within their province's share. Your university usually helps you request it. Students going to Quebec need a CAQ instead, which plays the same role.

Since 1 January 2026, students starting a master's or doctoral degree at a public institution don't need a PAL. This doesn't cover graduate certificates and diplomas, or private institutions. Rules and allocations change from year to year, so confirm the current position with your university and on the IRCC website before you apply.

faqs.question: Are there scholarships for international students?
faqs.answer:
Yes, but competition is strong. The best-known are the Lester B. Pearson International Scholarship at the University of Toronto (a full undergraduate award, where your school nominates you), the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarships for PhD students (C$50,000 a year for three years, with a university nomination), and the UBC International Leader of Tomorrow award.

Most universities also give entrance awards to international students, from a few hundred to tens of thousands of dollars. Some are considered automatically when you apply, while others need a separate form and an earlier deadline, often in the autumn before your September start. Check each university's scholarship page early.

faqs.question: When should I start applying?
faqs.answer:
Start 9 to 12 months before your course begins. For a September start, many universities set deadlines between December and March, and some competitive programmes and scholarships close earlier. Colleges often run rolling admissions, but popular courses can fill up.

Once you have an offer, you'll need your attestation letter (if required), proof of funds and other documents for the study permit. Applying early leaves time to fix problems, which is useful because documents are sometimes queried.

faqs.question: Can I bring my spouse or children with me?
faqs.answer:
It depends on your level of study. A spouse or common-law partner can apply for an open work permit only if you are studying a master's degree of 16 months or longer, a doctoral degree, or one of a few eligible professional programmes. Spouses of undergraduate and college students generally cannot get one.

Dependent children can come to Canada and attend school. Your partner and children also need to meet the visa requirements and show extra funds. These rules have tightened recently, so check them before you choose a course if your family plans to join you.

faqs.question: Will I have health cover as an international student?
faqs.answer:
Health cover depends on the province, and it isn't automatic in the way it is in some countries. In Ontario, international students aren't covered by the public plan and are normally enrolled in the University Health Insurance Plan (UHIP). In British Columbia, you can join the public Medical Services Plan, but there can be a waiting period, so you'll need temporary private cover first.

Alberta offers public cover to eligible students on longer permits, and in Quebec many schools enrol international students in a group plan. Universities also run extended health and dental plans for things like prescriptions. Check what your university and province provide before you arrive.

faqs.question: Where will I live, and how much will it cost?
faqs.answer:
Many first-year students live in university residence, which is the simplest option, and many universities guarantee a place to new students who apply by the deadline. After that, most students share a rented flat or house, or rent a room in a family home.

Rent is the biggest part of your budget and varies a lot by city: it is highest in Vancouver and Toronto and often lower in smaller cities. Apply for residence as early as you can, and be careful with online listings, since rental scams are common. Never send money before you've seen a place or checked the landlord.

faqs.question: What if my study permit is refused?
faqs.answer:
A refusal isn't always the end of the road. The refusal letter explains why, so read it carefully and tell your university. Common reasons include unclear study plans, weak proof of funds or missing documents.

Most students fix the weak point and apply again with a stronger application and a clear explanation of why they chose their programme. In some cases you can ask the Federal Court to review the decision, but it is slow and the deadlines are short, so get advice quickly if you want to go that way.

faqs.question: Can I apply on my own, or do I need a consultancy?
faqs.answer:
You can absolutely apply on your own. Universities accept direct applications and the study permit is applied for on the official IRCC website, and plenty of students do it themselves.

The catch is that there are many moving parts: choosing the right province and programme, meeting deadlines, getting an attestation letter, preparing proof of funds and writing a convincing study plan. Small mistakes are a common reason for delays or refusals. If you'd like a second pair of eyes on your plan, you can book an appointment with our team.

courses.guidanceIntro: Canada offers thousands of undergraduate, college and postgraduate programmes. When choosing a course, it helps to think about your academic and career goals, whether the programme offers co-op or work placements, and which province suits your budget and lifestyle.
guidanceQuestions: What subject are you most interested in, and how does it fit your future plans?
Does the programme include a co-op term, internship or work placement?
Is the institution a designated learning institution, and does the programme qualify for a Post-Graduation Work Permit?
What are the entry and language requirements for your level of study?
Which province and city fit your budget, and what do current students say about them?

preview.heading: Study in a Country Known for Its Welcome
preview.paragraph:
Canada has high-quality universities and colleges spread across ten provinces and three territories, from big, busy cities to quieter campus towns. You can pick a setting that fits how you want to live, and study in English, in French, or in both.

Outside the classroom you'll find a safe, multicultural society, well-run public services, and plenty of open space for weekends away.

details.introParagraph: Beyond the strong teaching and well-regarded degrees, there is a lot to like about life in Canada. It is a country built by people from all over the world, and that shows in its neighbourhoods, food, festivals and everyday attitudes. Cities are safe and easy to settle into, public transport is widespread, and nature is never far away, whether that means a lake, a mountain trail or a quiet beach. Winters are cold, but campuses and cities are well set up for them, and most international students find the welcome warmer than the weather.

highlight.title: Provinces and Territories
highlight.body:
Canada is made up of ten provinces and three territories, each with its own character, climate and, in some cases, language. Most international students study in Ontario and British Columbia, home to cities like Toronto, Ottawa and Vancouver, but Quebec, Alberta, Nova Scotia and the Prairie provinces all have strong institutions and often lower living costs.

Education is run by each province, so tuition, health cover and the rules for attestation letters can differ depending on where you study. It's worth comparing provinces, not just universities, before you apply.

topics.title: Food
topics.body:
Canadian food is a mix of local favourites and flavours from around the world. You'll find poutine, maple syrup treats, butter tarts and Nanaimo bars, but also excellent South Asian, East Asian, Middle Eastern, Caribbean and African food in almost every big city. Halal, kosher and vegetarian options are easy to find in most university cities.

Student budgets stretch furthest if you cook at home. Supermarkets such as Walmart, No Frills and Costco keep everyday groceries affordable, and many campuses have student-priced cafés and food banks. A typical grocery budget is around C$200 to C$600 a month, depending on how often you eat out.

topics.title: Weather
topics.body:
Canada has four clear seasons. Summers are warm and sunny, autumn brings brilliant colours, and winters can be properly cold and snowy, especially in Ontario, Quebec and the Prairies, where temperatures often fall well below freezing. The Pacific coast, including Vancouver, is milder but wetter.

If you come from a warmer country, the first winter takes some adjusting to. A good winter coat, insulated waterproof boots, gloves and layers you can add or remove are worth buying early. Many cities, such as Toronto and Montreal, also have indoor walkways and underground networks that make winter days easier.

topics.title: Religion
topics.body:
Canada is a multi-faith, largely secular society where freedom of religion is protected and people of many beliefs live side by side. Most university cities have mosques, temples, gurdwaras, churches, synagogues and other places of worship within reach of campus, and student unions often run faith and cultural societies.

Campuses are generally well set up for religious students, with prayer and multi-faith spaces, chaplaincy services and dietary options in dining halls. It's worth checking the services at your specific university once you have an offer.

topics.title: Travel and Transport
topics.body:
Canada is huge, but getting around your own city is straightforward. Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and most other cities have buses, trains or subways, and many universities include a transit pass in student fees or offer a discounted one. A monthly transit pass is usually in the range of C$80 to C$150.

For trips between cities, distances are long, so most students use trains, intercity coaches or low-cost flights, and plan bigger trips for holidays. Most students don't need a car, and winter driving takes real experience, so it's best to wait until you know the area.

topics.title: Language
topics.body:
English and French are both official languages. Across most of Canada daily life and teaching happen in English, while Quebec is mainly French-speaking, and cities like Montreal, Ottawa and parts of New Brunswick are bilingual.

Most international students study in English, and several universities in Quebec teach in French. Learning some French can help with jobs and day-to-day life in those areas, and either language can be used to prove your level for study and work permits.

topics.title: Holidays
topics.body:
The Canadian calendar is full of celebrations worth planning around: Canada Day on 1 July, Thanksgiving in October, Remembrance Day on 11 November, Christmas and New Year, plus provincial holidays such as Family Day in February and Victoria Day in May. There are also local festivals, winter carnivals and music events almost every month.

Universities build a break around the winter holidays and a short reading week in the middle of term, which gives international students a natural window to travel or rest. The long summer break is a good chance to work, take a co-op placement or explore the country.

whyStudy.summary: Beyond the rankings, here's what matters day to day: what it costs to live, how much you can work while you study, and what you can do after you graduate.

reasons.heading: High-Quality Universities and Colleges, Respected Worldwide
reasons.body:
Canada is home to well-known research universities such as the University of Toronto, McGill and the University of British Columbia, alongside colleges that focus on practical, career-ready training. Employers around the world recognise Canadian qualifications, and teaching tends to be discussion-based, with plenty of group work and independent thinking.

Whether you want a research-heavy degree or a hands-on diploma, there is a route that fits, and many programmes let you build in work experience along the way.

reasons.heading: Good Value, Especially at Graduate Level
reasons.body:
Tuition depends a lot on the province and the programme. Statistics Canada's 2025/26 figures put the average for international undergraduates at about C$41,746 a year and for international graduate students at about C$24,028. Averages range widely: roughly C$18,867 for undergraduates in Newfoundland and Labrador, compared with about C$49,802 in Ontario.

That means choosing your province and programme carefully can change your total cost a great deal, and smaller cities often have lower rent too.

reasons.heading: Work While You Study
reasons.body:
If your study permit allows it, you can work off campus for up to 24 hours a week during term and full-time during scheduled breaks, and on-campus work is also possible. That can cover some day-to-day costs and give you real Canadian work experience before you graduate.

It isn't enough to fund your studies on its own, so treat it as a supplement. Always check your study permit conditions before you start a job.

reasons.heading: A Clear Route to Work After Graduation
reasons.body:
Many graduates can apply for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP), which can last up to three years depending on the length of your programme. Graduates of a master's degree can receive the full three years even if the programme was shorter than two years, as long as they meet the other requirements.

Bachelor's, master's and doctoral graduates do not have to meet the field-of-study list, but you do need to prove your English or French level, and you can only receive one PGWP in your lifetime. Canadian work experience can also help later if you want to apply to stay long-term.

reasons.heading: A Safe, Welcoming, Multicultural Home
reasons.body:
Canada is one of the most diverse countries in the world, and international students quickly find classmates, food, festivals and communities from their own part of the world. Most campuses run orientation programmes, peer mentors and student services built around newcomers.

Cities are generally safe, public services work well, and people tend to be friendly and polite, which makes the first few weeks far easier.

reasons.heading: Study in English, French, or Both
reasons.body:
Canada has two official languages, which gives you choices most countries can't. Most students study in English, but you can also study in French in Quebec and bilingual regions, and many students pick up some French along the way.

Being able to work in two international languages is a real advantage on your CV, whether you stay in Canada or return home.

reasons.heading: Hands-On Learning and Industry Links
reasons.body:
Many Canadian programmes include co-op terms, internships or required work placements, so you graduate with experience as well as a degree. This is especially common in engineering, business, computer science and health programmes.

Recent rule changes mean most post-secondary international students no longer need a separate co-op work permit for placements that are a required part of their programme, but always confirm the details with your university's international office.

sections.title: Cost of Living
sections.summary: From 1 September 2026, a single study permit applicant must show C$23,448 for living costs, which works out to roughly C$1,950 a month, and many students spend more in Vancouver and Toronto.
sections.body: Rent is usually the biggest expense, and it varies a lot by city: it is highest in Vancouver and Toronto and generally lower in smaller cities. Food is often C$200 to C$600 a month, and a monthly transit pass is usually C$80 to C$150. Quebec sets its own, higher proof-of-funds amount for study permits, so students heading there should check the Quebec rules. Budget for your first month carefully, since landlords often ask for a deposit or advance rent.

sections.title: Part-time Job Opportunities
sections.summary: Eligible students can work up to 24 hours a week off campus during term, and full-time during scheduled breaks.
sections.body: Common student jobs include retail, hospitality, campus roles and tutoring. The 24-hour limit is strict, and working more than your permit allows can put your status at risk, so keep a record of your hours. Work is only allowed if your study permit says so, and you can't start working before your programme begins. Part-time income rarely covers all living costs, so it works best as a supplement.

sections.title: After Graduation
sections.summary: Graduates can apply for a Post-Graduation Work Permit of up to three years, depending on programme length.
sections.body: To qualify for a PGWP you need to graduate from an eligible programme at a designated learning institution, study full time, and meet the language requirement (CLB 7 for university degrees, CLB 5 for college programmes). You must apply within 180 days of getting confirmation that you've completed your programme. Career services at most Canadian universities offer CV help, interview practice and employer events, which are worth using well before your final term.

topCourses.name: Computer Science and Information Technology
topCourses.body: Computer science and IT programmes cover programming, software development, data analysis and cybersecurity, and most also include databases, networks, algorithms and a growing amount of artificial intelligence and machine learning. Universities usually teach the theory and mathematics behind computing, while colleges tend to focus on applied, job-ready IT skills, so it's worth deciding which style suits you. Many programmes include co-op terms or a final project built with a real client, and the maths and logic you build here transfer to almost any technical field.

topCourses.name: Engineering
topCourses.body: Engineering programmes cover civil, mechanical, electrical, chemical, aerospace and software engineering, among others. Many universities start with a shared first year of maths, physics and design, then let you choose a specialisation, and learning is a mix of lectures, labs and team design projects, often finishing with a capstone project. It helps to choose a programme accredited by Engineers Canada, since that matters if you later want to become a licensed professional engineer. A strong background in maths and physics makes the first years much easier.

topCourses.name: Business and Management
topCourses.body: Business and management programmes focus on leadership, finance, marketing and entrepreneurship, and many also include operations, human resources, supply chain and business analytics. Teaching is usually case-based, with a lot of group work, presentations and real company projects, and you can study it as a bachelor's degree, a college diploma or a master's such as an MBA. Many programmes let you specialise in your second or third year, and co-op or internship options are common.

topCourses.name: Health Sciences (Nursing, Pharmacy, Medicine)
topCourses.body: Health sciences is a broad area that includes nursing, pharmacy, medicine and related fields such as biomedical science, public health and rehabilitation. These programmes combine science courses with supervised clinical placements, so you learn in hospitals and clinics as well as in the classroom. Professional paths such as nursing and pharmacy lead to a licensing exam set by each province, and most medical schools take very few international students, so it's wise to look at related degrees as well. Strong results in biology and chemistry are usually expected.

topCourses.name: Finance and Accounting
topCourses.body: Finance and accounting programmes teach financial management, auditing and investment analysis, along with taxation, financial reporting and risk management. Accounting degrees are often designed to meet part of the education requirements for professional designations such as the CPA, and finance programmes often prepare you for exams like the CFA. The subject is quantitative and detail-focused, so it suits students who enjoy numbers, spreadsheets and structured problem-solving.

topCourses.name: Environmental Science and Sustainability
topCourses.body: These programmes focus on sustainable practices and environmental conservation, and they bring together ecology, climate science, water and soil studies, renewable energy and environmental policy. Canada's forests, coastlines, lakes and Arctic landscapes make it a strong place for fieldwork, and many courses include time outdoors and lab work, plus tools such as mapping and data analysis (GIS). It suits students who like science but also want to work on real-world questions such as climate and resource management.

topCourses.name: Arts and Humanities
topCourses.body: Arts and humanities programmes explore human culture, history, literature, philosophy and languages, and they build critical thinking, research and writing skills. Teaching is based on seminars, reading and essays, with plenty of discussion, and areas such as linguistics, creative writing and Indigenous studies are often available too. Most universities let you combine a major with a minor in another subject, which makes the degree flexible if you're still deciding where your interests lie.

topCourses.name: Hospitality and Tourism Management
topCourses.body: Hospitality and tourism programmes teach hotel and resort operations, event planning, food and beverage management and tourism marketing. They are strongly practical, with training in simulated hotels and kitchens, group projects, and often a work placement as part of the course. You can study it as a college diploma or as a degree, and the course suits students who enjoy working with people and organising experiences.

topCourses.name: International Relations and Political Science
topCourses.body: This area looks at global politics, diplomacy and international affairs, and covers political theory, comparative politics, international law, security and human rights. Teaching is built around reading, debate and research papers, and studying in Canada gives you access to a bilingual capital, Ottawa, which is home to government institutions, embassies and think tanks. It suits students who enjoy analysing how countries and institutions make decisions.

topCourses.name: Education and Early Childhood Development
topCourses.body: Education programmes focus on teaching methods, child development and curriculum design, and include learning theory, inclusive classrooms and supervised practice in schools or childcare settings. Early childhood programmes are often offered as college diplomas or degrees, while teacher education in many provinces is a degree taken after a first degree. Becoming a licensed teacher requires certification from the province where you want to work, so it's worth checking those rules early.

Research degrees may also need a supervisor to agree to take you on, and professional programmes can have extra requirements.

faqs.question: What if my study permit is refused?
faqs.answer:
A refusal isn't always the end of the road. The refusal letter explains why, so read it carefully and tell your university. Common reasons include unclear study plans, weak proof of funds or missing documents.

Most students fix the weak point and apply again with a stronger application and a clear explanation of why they chose their programme. In some cases you can ask the Federal Court to review the decision, but it is slow and the deadlines are short, so get advice quickly if you want to go that way.

faqs.question: Can I apply on my own, or do I need a consultancy?
faqs.answer:
You can absolutely apply on your own. Universities accept direct applications and the study permit is applied for on the official IRCC website, and plenty of students do it themselves.

The catch is that there are many moving parts: choosing the right province and programme, meeting deadlines, getting an attestation letter, preparing proof of funds and writing a convincing study plan. Small mistakes are a common reason for delays or refusals. If you'd like a second pair of eyes on your plan, you can book an appointment with our team.

courses.guidanceIntro: Canada offers thousands of undergraduate, college and postgraduate programmes. When choosing a course, it helps to think about your academic and career goals, whether the programme offers co-op or work placements, and which province suits your budget and lifestyle.
guidanceQuestions: What subject are you most interested in, and how does it fit your future plans?
Does the programme include a co-op term, internship or work placement?
Is the institution a designated learning institution, and does the programme qualify for a Post-Graduation Work Permit?
What are the entry and language requirements for your level of study?
Which province and city fit your budget, and what do current students say about them?
